questions.subject: ICU Procedures & Monitoring
questions.question:
Which of the following is an absolute contraindication to performing Transesophageal 
Echocardiography (TEE)?
options: History of radiation to the mediastinum
questions.explanation: Transesophageal Echocardiography (TEE) involves blind instrumentation of the esophagus with a rigid transducer probe. Absolute contraindications include pathology causing esophageal obstruction or mucosal disruption with high risk of perforation: severe esophageal stricture, esophageal tumor, active esophageal perforation or laceration (Boerhaave/Mallory-Weiss), active upper GI hemorrhage, or recent upper GI/esophageal surgery.

whyWrong.A: Severe aortic stenosis is an indication for TEE (assessing valve area and anatomy), not a contraindication.
whyWrong.B: Correct: Esophageal stricture / perforation is an absolute contraindication to TEE due to risk of rupture.
whyWrong.C: Atrial fibrillation is a primary indication for TEE (ruling out left atrial appendage thrombus before cardioversion).
whyWrong.D: Severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction is an indication for TEE monitoring.

questions.examPearl:
HIGH-YIELD TAKEAWAYS:
• Absolute TEE contraindications: Esophageal stricture, perforation, diverticulum (Zenker), active GI bleeding, recent esophageal surgery.
• Relative contraindications: Cervical spine instability, severe coagulopathy, esophageal varices (Grade 3/4).

questions.subject: Hematology & Transfusion
questions.question: Massive transfusion is defined as administration of which of the following?
options: 1 unit of PRBC every hour for 24 hours
questions.explanation: Massive transfusion (MT) is classically defined as the transfusion of 10 or more units of Packed Red Blood Cells (PRBCs) within a 24-hour period, which roughly approximates replacement of the patient's entire circulating blood volume. Modern operational definitions also include transfusion of >= 4–5 units of PRBCs within 1 hour, or >= 10 units of total blood products in 24 hours.

whyWrong.A: Correct: Transfusion of >= 10 units of PRBC in 24 hours is the classic standard definition of massive transfusion.
whyWrong.B: 4 units in 24 hours is standard transfusion, not massive transfusion.
whyWrong.C: 20 units in 24 hours is ultra-massive transfusion.
whyWrong.D: 2 units within 12 hours is routine non-massive transfusion.

questions.examPearl:
HIGH-YIELD TAKEAWAYS:
• Massive Transfusion Protocol (MTP): Activated for >= 10 units PRBC/24h or >= 4 units/1h with ongoing bleeding.
• Balanced 1:1:1 ratio (PRBC : FFP : Platelets) alongside early tranexamic acid (TXA within 3 hours) and calcium repletion.

questions.subject: Resuscitation & Airway
questions.question: Central cyanosis may be masked in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: Central cyanosis becomes clinically apparent when deoxygenated hemoglobin in capillary blood exceeds 5 g/dL (corresponding roughly to SaO2 < 85% at normal hemoglobin). In Carbon Monoxide (CO) poisoning, carboxyhemoglobin imparts a bright cherry-red color to blood and skin, so patients remain pink or flushed despite profound cellular hypoxia and tissue asphyxiation. Severe anemia also masks cyanosis because total hemoglobin may be too low to reach 5 g/dL of deoxygenated hemoglobin.

whyWrong.A: Polycythemia accentuates cyanosis at higher oxygen saturations because absolute deoxyhemoglobin easily exceeds 5 g/dL.
whyWrong.B: High altitude increases deoxygenation, making cyanosis more apparent.
whyWrong.C: Hypothermia causes peripheral vasoconstriction, promoting peripheral cyanosis.
whyWrong.D: Correct: Carbon monoxide poisoning causes 'cherry-red' blood and masks central cyanosis despite lethal tissue hypoxia.

questions.examPearl:
HIGH-YIELD TAKEAWAYS:
• Cyanosis requires >= 5 g/dL of deoxygenated hemoglobin. Severe anemia (< 6 g/dL) CANNOT manifest cyanosis.
• Carbon monoxide poisoning masks cyanosis (carboxyhemoglobin gives cherry-red color); standard pulse oximetry falsely reads 100%.

questions.subject: Toxicology
questions.question:
Which of the following is recommended as prophylaxis before administering Anti-Snake 
Venom (ASV) to reduce the risk of early anaphylactic reactions?
questions.explanation: Early adverse reactions (anaphylactoid/anaphylactic reactions) to horse-derived Anti-Snake Venom (ASV) occur in 20–50% of patients. Prophylactic low-dose Subcutaneous or Intramuscular Adrenaline (epinephrine 0.25 mg SC/IM in adults, 0.005–0.01 mg/kg in children) administered 10–15 minutes before ASV infusion significantly reduces the incidence of severe early anaphylactic reactions (proven in randomized controlled trials). Antihistamines and hydrocortisone show significantly lower prophylactic efficacy.

whyWrong.A: Correct: Subcutaneous adrenaline is the evidence-based prophylactic agent that prevents severe early ASV hypersensitivity.
whyWrong.B: Intravenous atropine does not prevent immunoglobulin-mediated anaphylactoid reactions.
whyWrong.C: Oral paracetamol has no prophylactic effect on anaphylactic shock.
whyWrong.D: High-dose furosemide has no role in ASV prophylaxis and worsens hemoconcentration/hypotension.

questions.examPearl:
HIGH-YIELD TAKEAWAYS:
• WHO snakebite guidelines: Prophylactic subcutaneous adrenaline (0.25 mg) reduces severe early adverse reactions to ASV.
• If severe anaphylactoid reaction develops: Stop ASV infusion immediately, give IM adrenaline (0.5 mg), and resume ASV slowly once resolved.

questions.subject: Nutrition & GI
questions.question:
Which of the following is the most sensitive and specific biochemical marker for diagnosing 
acute pancreatitis?
questions.explanation: Serum Lipase is the most sensitive (85–100%) and specific (95–100%) biochemical marker for acute pancreatitis. Lipase rises within 4–8 hours of onset, peaks at 24 hours, and remains elevated for 8–14 days. Serum amylase rises early but clears within 3–5 days, has lower specificity (elevated in salivary disease, appendicitis, bowel obstruction, renal failure), and may be normal in hypertriglyceridemic or delayed presentations.

whyWrong.A: Correct: Serum lipase has superior sensitivity, specificity, and longer diagnostic window than amylase.
whyWrong.B: Serum amylase is less specific and normalizes rapidly within 3–5 days.
whyWrong.C: Serum alkaline phosphatase reflects biliary obstruction, not parenchymal pancreatic inflammation.
whyWrong.D: Serum transaminases reflect hepatocellular injury, though ALT > 150 IU/L suggests a biliary etiology.

questions.examPearl:
HIGH-YIELD TAKEAWAYS:
• Revised Atlanta criteria: Diagnosis requires 2 of 3: 1) Characteristic epigastric pain, 2) Serum lipase or amylase > 3x ULN, 3) Imaging features.
• Lipase is preferred over amylase due to higher clinical accuracy and longer diagnostic window.

questions.subject: Neurocritical Care
questions.question: Which of the following clinical features is true regarding Bell's palsy?
options: Inability to close the eye on the affected side
questions.explanation: Bell's palsy is an acute idiopathic peripheral lower motor neuron (LMN) facial palsy (Cranial Nerve VII). Because the frontalis muscle receives bilateral cortical upper motor neuron innervation, an LMN lesion paralyzes the ENTIRE ipsilateral half of the face, including the forehead (inability to wrinkle the forehead, lagophthalmos, drooping corner of mouth). In contrast, an upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion (e.g. stroke) spares the forehead.

whyWrong.A: Correct: Bell's palsy involves LMN facial palsy with inability to wrinkle the forehead on the ipsilateral side.
whyWrong.B: Forehead sparing is the classic hallmark of central upper motor neuron (UMN) stroke lesions.
whyWrong.C: Preserved taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is variable; chorda tympani involvement frequently causes taste impairment.
whyWrong.D: Contralateral lower facial weakness describes a unilateral cerebral hemispheric stroke, not peripheral Bell's palsy.

questions.examPearl:
HIGH-YIELD TAKEAWAYS:
• Facial palsy rule: LMN lesion (Bell's palsy) = Forehead INVOLVED (cannot wrinkle brow).
• UMN lesion (Stroke) = Forehead SPARED (can wrinkle brow due to bilateral cortical innervation).

questions.chapter: Non-Invasive Ventilation & High Flow Nasal Cannula
questions.subject: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.question: In a patient with ARDS, which of the following is the most common cause for NIV failure?
questions.explanation: Non-invasive ventilation (NIV) has high failure rates (up to 50–70%) in de novo acute hypoxemic respiratory failure and moderate-to-severe ARDS. The most important predictor of NIV failure is severe baseline hypoxemia (PaO2/FiO2 < 150 mmHg) and large tidal volume generation (> 9–9.5 mL/kg PBW). High transpulmonary pressure swings cause Patient-Self-Inflicted Lung Injury (P-SILI). HACOR score > 5 at 1 hour also strongly predicts NIV failure.

whyWrong.A: Mild hypercapnia in COPD is an indication FOR non-invasive ventilation, with high success rates.
whyWrong.B: Correct: Severe hypoxemia (P/F < 150) is the leading determinant of NIV failure in ARDS.
whyWrong.C: Age alone is not the primary physiological driver of acute NIV failure.
whyWrong.D: Uncomplicated respiratory alkalosis from early mild anxiety does not drive NIV failure.

questions.examPearl:
HIGH-YIELD TAKEAWAYS:
• NIV in ARDS: High failure rate if PaO2/FiO2 < 150 mmHg. Delayed intubation significantly increases mortality.
• Use HACOR score (HR, Acidosis, Consciousness, Oxygenation, RR) at 1 hour: Score > 5 indicates > 80% risk of failure.

questions.chapter: ICU Management of Traumatic Brain Injury
questions.subject: Neurocritical Care
questions.question: Which of the following clinical patterns is characteristic of Brown-Sequard syndrome?
options: Bilateral loss of all sensations below the lesion
Ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature with contralateral motor weakness
Ipsilateral motor loss with contralateral pain and temperature loss
Only lower limb weakness without sensory loss
questions.explanation: Brown-Sequard syndrome results from hemisection of the spinal cord (e.g. penetrating trauma). Classical presentation consists of: 1) Ipsilateral motor loss below the lesion (corticospinal tract); 2) Ipsilateral loss of fine touch, vibration, and proprioception below the lesion (dorsal column-medial lemniscal tract); and 3) Contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation beginning 1–2 segments below the lesion (spinothalamic tract, which decussates 1-2 levels above entry).

whyWrong.A: Bilateral motor and sensory loss describes complete spinal cord transection.
whyWrong.B: Ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature is anatomically incorrect because the spinothalamic tract decussates in the anterior white commissure.
whyWrong.C: Correct: Ipsilateral motor + proprioception loss with contralateral pain + temperature loss.
whyWrong.D: Dissociated sensory loss with preserved motor function occurs in central cord syndrome / syringomyelia.

questions.examPearl:
HIGH-YIELD TAKEAWAYS:
• Brown-Sequard syndrome: IPSILATERAL motor paralysis & vibration/proprioception loss + CONTRALATERAL pain & temperature loss.
• Most common etiology: Penetrating trauma (stab wound / gunshot wound) or asymmetric disk herniation.

questions.subject: Infectious Diseases
questions.question:
Which antiseptic agent is recommended for skin preparation prior to performing invasive 
procedures?
questions.explanation: CDC and international infection control guidelines recommend an alcoholic chlorhexidine solution (> 0.5% or 2% chlorhexidine gluconate in 70% isopropyl alcohol) as the preferred antiseptic agent for skin preparation prior to central venous catheter (CVC) insertion and during dressing changes. Alcoholic chlorhexidine provides superior rapid bactericidal activity, persistent residual antimicrobial activity (binding stratum corneum), and significantly lower rates of Central Line-Associated Bloodstream Infection (CLABSI) compared to povidone-iodine.

whyWrong.A: Correct: 2% Chlorhexidine gluconate in 70% isopropyl alcohol is the gold-standard skin antiseptic.
whyWrong.B: Aqueous povidone-iodine requires longer contact drying time (2 min) and has less persistent residual activity.
whyWrong.C: 70% ethyl alcohol alone evaporates rapidly without persistent residual bactericidal effect.
whyWrong.D: Hydrogen peroxide causes tissue irritation and lacks broad residual antibacterial efficacy.

questions.examPearl:
HIGH-YIELD TAKEAWAYS:
• CLABSI bundle: Alcoholic chlorhexidine (>0.5% or 2% in 70% alcohol), full sterile barrier precautions, subclavian vein preference, daily line necessity review.
• Allow chlorhexidine to dry completely (air dry for at least 2 minutes) before vascular puncture.

questions.subject: Infectious Diseases
questions.question:
Which of the following is the most important risk factor for developing Clostridioides difficile 
infection (CDI) in ICU patients?
options: Stress ulcer prophylaxis with H2 blockers
questions.explanation: Prior or ongoing exposure to broad-spectrum antibiotics is the single most important and potent risk factor for developing Clostridioides difficile infection. Antibiotic therapy disrupts normal protective colonic microbiota, facilitating C. difficile spore germination, vegetative growth, and production of toxin A (enterotoxin) and toxin B (cytotoxin). Highest-risk antibiotics include fluoroquinolones, 3rd/4th generation cephalosporins, clindamycin, and broad-spectrum beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitors.

whyWrong.A: Young age is protective; advanced age (>= 65 years) is a major risk factor.
whyWrong.B: Exclusive high-fiber diet does not induce C. difficile dysbiosis.
whyWrong.C: Correct: Broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy is the paramount risk factor for C. difficile colitis.
whyWrong.D: Short hospital stay carries low risk; prolonged hospitalization markedly increases exposure to spores.

questions.examPearl:
HIGH-YIELD TAKEAWAYS:
• C. difficile risk factors: Broad-spectrum antibiotics (Fluoroquinolones, Clindamycin, Cephalosporins), PPIs, age > 65, prolonged hospitalization.
• First-line treatment: Oral Fidaxomicin (200 mg BID for 10 days) or oral Vancomycin (125 mg QID for 10 days). Metronidazole is no longer first-line.

questions.subject: Trauma & Burns
questions.question:
REBOA (Resuscitative Endovascular Balloon Occlusion of the Aorta) is most beneficial in 
controlling bleeding from which of the following sites?
questions.explanation: REBOA (Resuscitative Endovascular Balloon Occlusion of the Aorta) occludes the aorta at specific anatomic zones to arrest non-compressible torso hemorrhage: Zone 1: Descending thoracic aorta (left subclavian to celiac axis, ~T4-T10) for subdiaphragmatic/intra-abdominal hemorrhage; Zone 2: Paravisceral aorta (celiac to lowest renal artery) - NO OCCLUSION ZONE; Zone 3: Infrarenal abdominal aorta (lowest renal artery to aortic bifurcation, ~L1-L4) - used specifically for severe pelvic fracture hemorrhage and junctional groin bleeding.

whyWrong.A: Zone 1 is used for massive intra-abdominal hemorrhage or cardiac arrest.
whyWrong.B: Zone 2 is the paravisceral aorta (mesenteric/renal arteries) and is strictly a non-occlusion zone.
whyWrong.C: Ascending aorta occlusion is not performed with REBOA.
whyWrong.D: Correct: Zone 3 (infrarenal aorta) is indicated for severe pelvic fracture hemorrhage and junctional groin trauma.

questions.examPearl:
HIGH-YIELD TAKEAWAYS:
• REBOA zones: Zone 1 = Thoracic aorta (intra-abdominal hemorrhage); Zone 2 = Visceral (NO occlusion); Zone 3 = Infrarenal (pelvic fracture hemorrhage).
• Zone 3 occlusion maintains visceral and renal perfusion while controlling pelvic bleeding.

questions.subject: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.question:
Which of the following is the hemodynamic effect of applying positive end-expiratory 
pressure (PEEP)?
options: Afterload of the right ventricle decreases
questions.explanation: Application of Positive End-Expiratory Pressure (PEEP) increases mean intrathoracic pressure, which decreases systemic venous return (decreasing right ventricular preload) and increases pulmonary vascular resistance by compressing alveolar capillary microvessels (increasing right ventricular afterload). This combination decreases RV stroke volume and shifts the interventricular septum leftward (ventricular interdependence), resulting in decreased left ventricular preload and a subsequent decrease in cardiac output.

whyWrong.A: Correct: PEEP decreases RV preload and increases RV afterload, ultimately decreasing cardiac output.
whyWrong.B: PEEP does not increase RV preload (it reduces venous return gradient).
whyWrong.C: PEEP does not decrease pulmonary vascular resistance in fully open lungs (high PEEP compresses alveolar capillaries).
whyWrong.D: PEEP does not systematically increase cardiac output in a normal heart.

questions.examPearl:
HIGH-YIELD TAKEAWAYS:
• Heart-lung interactions of PEEP: Increases intrathoracic pressure -> Decreases RV preload + Increases RV afterload -> Decreases Cardiac Output.
• Exception: In severe LV systolic failure / pulmonary edema, PEEP DECREASES LV afterload (transmural LV systolic pressure), which may augment stroke volume.

questions.subject: Hemodynamics
questions.question:
A 58-year-old woman develops sudden severe chest pain, dyspnea, and diaphoresis 
immediately after hearing about the unexpected death of her son. ECG shows ST-segment 
elevation, but coronary angiography reveals no obstructive lesions. What is the most likely 
diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (stress-induced cardiomyopathy / broken heart syndrome) is characterized by acute, transient left ventricular systolic dysfunction classically presenting as apical ballooning with basal hyperkinesis, triggered by intense emotional or physical stress. Presentation mimics acute myocardial infarction (chest pain, ST-elevation, elevated troponins), but coronary angiography demonstrates absence of obstructive coronary artery disease.

whyWrong.A: Acute anterior STEMI demonstrates obstructive plaque rupture on coronary angiography.
whyWrong.B: Correct: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy causes transient apical ballooning with non-obstructive coronary arteries.
whyWrong.C: Dilated cardiomyopathy causes chronic, non-transient global four-chamber dilation.
whyWrong.D: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a genetic disorder causing asymmetric septal hypertrophy.

questions.examPearl:
HIGH-YIELD TAKEAWAYS:
• Takotsubo cardiomyopathy: Stress trigger + ST elevation/troponin leak + Normal coronary arteries + Apical ballooning / basal hypercontractility.
• Pathophysiology: Massive catecholamine surge causing direct myocardial toxicity and microvascular spasm. >90% recover within 4–8 weeks.

questions.chapter: ICU Management of Traumatic Brain Injury
questions.subject: Neurocritical Care
questions.question:
Which of the following is a typical clinical feature of Anterior Cerebral Artery (ACA) 
syndrome?
questions.explanation: The Anterior Cerebral Artery (ACA) supplies the medial aspect of the cerebral hemisphere, including the motor and sensory homunculus corresponding to the contralateral lower extremity and genitalia, as well as the anterior frontal lobe. Consequently, an ACA stroke characteristically produces contralateral motor and sensory loss that is predominantly in the LOWER extremity (leg > arm/face), accompanied by abulia, akinetic mutism, and urinary incontinence.

whyWrong.A: Contralateral hemiparesis affecting the face and arm more than the leg is the classic hallmark of Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA) stroke.
whyWrong.B: Correct: ACA infarction causes contralateral hemiparesis and sensory deficit affecting the lower extremity significantly more than the upper extremity.
whyWrong.C: Ipsilateral cranial nerve deficits with contralateral hemiparesis indicates a brainstem stroke (crossed paralysis).
whyWrong.D: Homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing indicates Posterior Cerebral Artery (PCA) stroke.

questions.examPearl:
HIGH-YIELD TAKEAWAYS:
• Stroke syndromes: ACA = Leg > Face/Arm; MCA = Face/Arm > Leg + Aphasia (dominant) / Neglect (non-dominant); PCA = Visual deficits (hemianopia).
• Bilateral ACA infarction can occur with an unpaired (azygos) anterior cerebral artery, causing paraplegia and akinetic mutism.

questions.subject: Sepsis
questions.question:
A 64-year-old woman is admitted with altered sensorium, fever (39.5°C), tachycardia 
(132/min), and warm extremities. BP is 86/52 mmHg despite broad-spectrum antibiotics. 
Urine output over the last 3 hours is only 10 mL (oliguria). Lactate is 4.8 mmol/L. On bedside 
assessment, she shows improvement in blood pressure with a passive leg raise test (fluid 
responsive). 
What is the most appropriate immediate management?
questions.explanation: In septic shock with persistent hypotension or hyperlactatemia (lactate >= 4 mmol/L), the Surviving Sepsis Campaign recommends an initial fluid bolus of 30 mL/kg of balanced crystalloids within the first 3 hours. If mean arterial pressure remains < 65 mmHg during or immediately after fluid loading, vasopressor therapy (Norepinephrine) must be initiated promptly without delay to maintain vital organ perfusion pressure.

whyWrong.A: Correct: Balanced crystalloid bolus followed by early vasopressor initiation if MAP remains < 65 mmHg is the standard evidence-based bundle.
whyWrong.B: Administering hypotonic dextrose fluids worsens tissue edema and fails to restore intravascular volume.
whyWrong.C: Withholding all fluids and relying solely on high-dose pure inotropes (dobutamine) causes severe tachycardia and worsens hypovolemic shock.
whyWrong.D: Waiting 12 hours before starting vasopressors results in prolonged hypoperfusion and irreversible ischemic multi-organ failure.

questions.examPearl:
HIGH-YIELD TAKEAWAYS:
• Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 bundle: 1) Measure lactate; 2) Obtain blood cultures before antibiotics; 3) Administer broad-spectrum antibiotics; 4) 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension/lactate >= 4; 5) Apply vasopressors (Norepinephrine) to maintain MAP >= 65.
• Early initiation of Norepinephrine (even via peripheral line temporarily) restores vascular tone and decreases capillary extravasation.

questions.subject: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.question: A 45-year-old intubated ARDS patient on VCV (Vt 6 mL/kg, PEEP 10 cmH2O) develops sudden peak airway pressure increase from 28 to 42 cmH2O. Plateau pressure remains unchanged at 24 cmH2O. What is the primary etiology?
options: Increased airway resistance (e.g., secretions, bronchospasm, endotracheal tube biting)
questions.explanation: Ppeak measures total pressure (resistive + elastic). Pplat measures elastic pressure of lungs and chest wall. An isolated rise in Ppeak with stable Pplat indicates an airway resistance problem.

whyWrong.A: Peak pressure increases while plateau remains constant, indicating increased resistive pressure (Ppeak - Pplat).
whyWrong.B: Decreased compliance increases both Ppeak and Pplat equally.
whyWrong.C: Auto-PEEP elevates baseline end-expiratory pressure and Pplat.
whyWrong.D: Increased intra-abdominal pressure decreases thoracoabdominal compliance, raising Pplat.

questions.examPearl:
HIGH-YIELD TAKEAWAYS:
• Peak - Plateau pressure gap > 4 cmH2O isolates airway resistance issues from parenchymal/compliance changes.

questions.question: In a patient with septic shock undergoing pulmonary artery catheterization, which parameters are expected in hyperdynamic phase?

questions.subject: Acid-Base Disorders
questions.subtopic: Normal Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis & Winter Formula
questions.question: A patient with severe diarrhea presents with pH 7.22, PaCO2 25 mmHg, HCO3- 10 mEq/L, Na+ 138, Cl- 114, K+ 3.2. What is the acid-base disorder?
options: Normal Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis (NAGMA) with appropriate respiratory compensation
questions.explanation: AG = 14 (Normal). Winter's formula: expected PaCO2 = (1.5 x 10) + 8 ± 2 = 23 ± 2. Actual PaCO2 is 25, fitting pure compensated NAGMA from GI bicarbonate loss.

whyWrong.A: AG = 138 - (114 + 10) = 14 (normal range 8-12 ± 4); Winter's formula target PaCO2 = 1.5(10)+8 ± 2 = 23 ± 2 mmHg.
whyWrong.B: Anion gap is normal.
whyWrong.C: Winter's formula confirms pure respiratory compensation.
whyWrong.D: Primary disorder is metabolic (pH 7.22, low HCO3-).

questions.examPearl:
HIGH-YIELD TAKEAWAYS:
• Diarrhea causes NAGMA (hyperchloremic). Winter's formula validates expected respiratory compensation PaCO2 = 1.5[HCO3-] + 8 ± 2.
